caption:
A furniture maker built 36 million tent pegs

At the start of the Second World War, Ercol's factory switched to war work. It made tent pegs from wood too small for other uses, and over the war it produced 36 million of them.

The catch? In 1944, the government's Board of Trade hired Ercol to make 100,000 low-cost Windsor chairs using English elm, a wood that was not generally used for furniture because it tended to warp. Ercolani developed a new drying process to fix that.

The payoff? A chair could be built from 14 pre-formed parts, and one could be made every 20 seconds. Mass-produced Ercol furniture then found a good market in post-war Britain. 🪑
